abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for understanding light transport in complex scenes by reformulating the rendering equation through the lens of functional analysis. Traditional approaches to global illumination rely on recursive integration over the hemisphere, which becomes computationally prohibitive for scenes with intricate occlusion and glossy surfaces. We propose representing light transport as a continuous operator in Hilbert space, enabling the application of spectral methods to approximate radiance distributions. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that this formulation naturally captures multi-bounce lighting phenomena while providing theoretical guarantees on approximation error. The framework reveals previously unexplored connections between rendering and other domains including quantum mechanics and financial mathematics. We prove that the eigenfunctions of the light transport operator correspond to modes of visual importance, offering fundamental insights into scene structure that inform future algorithm design. This paradigm shift moves beyond ray-based paradigms toward a mathematically rigorous treatment of image synthesis that unifies physically based rendering with data-driven approaches.

We present a rigorous theoretical analysis of variance reduction techniques in Monte Carlo rendering, deriving novel bounds that enable more effective importance sampling strategies. Previous work on metropolis light transport lacks theoretical grounding for practical parameter selection, leading to suboptimal performance in practice. Our analysis establishes explicit relationships between mutation parameters, proposal distributions, and convergence rates in terms of spectral properties of the scene's light transport operator. We prove that the widely-used balance heuristic for multiple importance sampling can be improved by incorporating covariance information between sampling techniques. The mathematical framework presented here characterizes the asymptotic behavior of misestimation in bidirectional path tracing, identifying previously unknown error sources in highly specular scenes. Based on these theoretical insights, we derive adaptive parameter selection criteria that guarantee faster convergence than state-of-the-art approaches. Experimental validation on challenging test scenes confirms that our theoretically-motivated sampling strategies reduce variance by 40-60% compared to existing heuristics while maintaining theoretical guarantees on estimator consistency.

We present Lumina, a novel real-time rendering system architecture designed for the emerging paradigm of neural visual computing. Unlike traditional rasterization pipelines, Lumina integrates differentiable rendering primitives directly into the GPU pipeline, enabling end-to-end optimization for downstream vision tasks. The system introduces a unified memory architecture that bridges traditional graphics buffers and neural network activations, allowing gradients to flow seamlessly between geometric representations and learned features. Our design supports real-time global illumination through a hybrid approach combining precomputed radiance transfer with neural upsampling, achieving interactive frame rates for complex environments. The system includes a custom shading language that compiles to both traditional GPU instructions and neural network inference paths, providing flexibility for hybrid rendering applications. We demonstrate Lumina's capabilities through applications including inverse rendering, neural texture synthesis, and real-time visual dubbing. The architecture opens new possibilities for interactive applications where traditional rendering constraints limit visual quality, representing a fundamental shift in how graphics systems are designed and used.

We describe MeshFlow Pro, a high-performance system for interactive geometry processing that achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing approaches through novel parallel algorithms. The system addresses the computational bottleneck in mesh deformation by introducing a hierarchical cages-based approach with dynamic load balancing across GPU compute units. Our implementation features a new mesh hierarchy construction algorithm that builds progressive representations optimized for streaming workloads, enabling processing of models with hundreds of millions of polygons at interactive rates. The system includes an advanced caching mechanism that exploits temporal coherence in animation sequences, reducing recomputation by up to 80% for typical deformation scenarios. We present a user-friendly API supporting popular geometry processing operations including Laplacian smoothing, parameterization, and interactive sculpting. Performance benchmarks demonstrate that MeshFlow Pro processes mesh editing operations 15-25x faster than OpenFlipper and libigl while maintaining numerical accuracy comparable to single-threaded implementations. The system's modular architecture supports straightforward extension for new algorithms, making it suitable as a platform for geometry processing research and production applications.
